title: A way back, and a saint who was only a name
intro: A reader wrote in the app's own Community tab that on iPhone, once you tap into a section, getting back sometimes means leaving the section altogether and finding your way down again. Sometimes undersold it. Eighty nine of the app's ninety nine screens had no way back at all, and on the website the browser's own back button had been covering for it, so it never showed up as a bug. Every one of those screens has one now. The rest of this release is the same kind of thing: work that was nearly finished and did not quite reach you. Seven prayer categories that said Planned and nothing else. A tab bar carrying seven tabs. A Spanish tab with no word on it. St Arsenius the Great, kept every May 8 and named on the day, with nothing behind his name. And five saints the calendar had been quietly listing twice. This release also carries the first of the Communion prayers, the day's commemoration on the Android home screen, and a sign up that can no longer hang.

sections.heading: A way back, on every screen
sections.body: The app had a back button and it was fitted per screen, which meant it was fitted on ten of them: five pages that carried their own header, and the five account pages that inherited one. The other eighty nine had nothing. On the website that never mattered, because the browser has its own back button and quietly stood in. Inside the app there is no browser and iPhone has no hardware back, so a reader who tapped from a saint into one of his writings was stuck there and had to leave through the tab bar and walk down again. That is what was reported and that is what is fixed. The button knows where it is: it stays off the tab screens, where back means nothing, and off the ten screens that already had one, so nothing shows two. If you opened the app straight onto a page from a link, where there is genuinely nothing behind you, it takes you to Today rather than doing nothing at all.

sections.heading: Six tabs, and the account moves to Discover
sections.body: The bottom bar carried seven tabs, which left each one about fifty eight pixels wide and made it the most crowded thing in the app. You has left the bar. Your account now sits in the Discover library as Settings, keeping the same gear it always wore so it reads as a move rather than a disappearance, and Discover stays lit while you are in there. Discover also lost its Featured today panel, which picked a topic and a council to show you. In the app that pick was frozen when the release was built, so the today in its name was never true there. Orthodox History was already in the Discover library and had been lighting no tab at all when you opened it. It does now.

sections.heading: Like on Community
sections.body: Posts and replies can be liked. Dislike is there too and it is recorded, so moderation has the signal, but only the like total is shown. A visible dislike tally on a prayer request invites exactly the pile on it measures, and a number people have already seen cannot be taken back. Pressing what you already pressed takes it back, and pressing the other one moves you across without making you undo the first. The count moves the moment you press and the server corrects it, so a slow connection never leaves a like on screen that was never recorded.

sections.heading: St Arsenius the Great
sections.body: He was kept on May 8 and named on the day, and there was no page behind the name. The Roman deacon whom Theodosius the Great chose to teach his sons, who left the palace for the desert of Scetis and became the Church's great teacher of silence: flee, be silent, pray always. He has a life now, and the sayings he is remembered by, including the one the fathers repeated most, that he had often repented of having spoken and never of having been silent. He is the one hundred and fifty eighth saint in the library. He carries no icon yet, so his page shows the same placeholder as the others still waiting for one.

sections.heading: Five saints were listed twice
sections.body: Adding Arsenius turned up a fault that had nothing to do with him. The calendar names some saints in plain text and links others to their page, and when a saint had a page but the day's entry had not been linked to it, the day showed him twice: once as text you could not tap, once as a link directly underneath. It was happening to St Silouan the Athonite on September 24, St Job of Pochaev on October 28, St Porphyrios of Kavsokalyvia on December 2 and St Herman of Alaska on December 13. St Paisius Velichkovsky was a different case: he had been entered twice on November 15 with two different notes. All five days now name each saint once, and the app will refuse to build if it ever happens again.

sections.heading: Planned prayers say what is coming
sections.body: Seven prayer categories are listed but not yet filled, because the text for them has to be a real public domain translation and nothing is ever invented to fill a gap. They were marked Planned and said nothing else, so tapping one did nothing and gave no reason. Each now says what it will hold: before work or study, after work, before travel, the Nativity fast, the fasts of the year, psalms for sickness and fear and sorrow, and thanksgiving. They still do not open, because there is still nothing to read. They will not describe a service that has not been sourced, and the app now refuses to build if one tries to.

sections.heading: The prayers before Communion
sections.body: A reader asked in Community for the prayers of preparation before receiving, and for the thanksgiving afterwards. The first half is here. Hapgood's Service Book prints six prayers of preparation and all six are in the app: St Basil the Great, St John Chrysostom, Simeon Metaphrastes, Simeon the New Theologian, St John of Damascus, and the short prayer said immediately before receiving. They are her words in her order, from the 1906 edition, which is out of copyright. Nothing was smoothed or modernised, and nothing was written to fill a gap. Where the scan had broken a word across a line, it was rejoined only where that same word stands unbroken elsewhere in the volume, and the ingest stops rather than guess at one it cannot find. The thanksgiving after Communion is not here yet. It will arrive the same way or not at all.

sections.heading: Eight places where the scan showed through
sections.body: Purify's texts are taken from scans of printed public-domain volumes, and where the scanning software cannot read a mark it prints something else in its place. Eight of those had reached the page. In the prayer of Simeon Metaphrastes, said in preparation for Communion, three questions stand one after another, and all three had lost their question marks: two black squares, a stray bracket and a hyphen were standing where they should have been, so a man asking what evil he has not done appeared instead to trail off. The same prayer ran two words together in the name of the Holy Spirit. St John of Damascus carried two stray carets in the middle of his sentences, left behind when the number of a footnote was taken out and the mark that pointed to it was not. A section of St Cyril on Luke was headed with the code for an ampersand rather than an ampersand. And the last note on the fourteenth chapter of Matthew ran on into the heading of the fifteenth, which is the same fault the last release took out of the Fathers' mouths in five other places. All eight are repaired against the volumes they came from rather than patched over, and every one was confirmed on the page before it was touched. The app now reads its whole library looking for that kind of damage, four thousand six hundred files of it, and refuses to build if it finds any.

sections.heading: The day's commemoration on your home screen
sections.body: Two readers asked for a widget. On Android there is one now: the saint the Church keeps today and whether the day is a fast, on the home screen, without opening the app. It follows the calendar you have chosen, so it says what the app says rather than a second opinion. It turns over at midnight where you are, not where the build machine was, and it survives a change of time zone. It needs no connection at all, because the whole year is worked out when the release is built and carried inside the app, four hundred days of it, so a reader who never updates still gets a correct day for longer than a release cycle. There is no iPhone widget yet. That one needs a separate piece of the app which does not exist today, and it is better to say so than to let it look forgotten.

sections.heading: Tab labels in your own language
sections.body: Three faults in the bar at the bottom, which is the most looked at text in the app. In Spanish the You tab had no word on it at all: the label was present but empty, which beats the fallback to English that a missing label would have got. Shop was written in English for everyone, in all twenty one languages, even though the word had been translated for every one of them. And Community had only ever been translated into English, so twenty languages showed the English word. All three are fixed, and the app now refuses to build if any label in any language is blank or falls back to English.

sections.heading: Sign up stops being able to hang
sections.body: A reader reported the page freezing while creating an account. Before an account is made, the app records that you accepted the terms, and it waits for that to be written. Nothing bounded the wait. On a poor connection the button could read Creating account until the browser itself gave up, which is a wait with no end and no way out of it. Inside the app it is worse, because that call crosses to the website and fails more often than the same call made on the site. The wait is now capped at twelve seconds, past a slow mobile round trip and well short of the point where somebody force quits. If it does not get through you are told to try again, which was always the only other outcome: sign up is deliberately stopped when acceptance cannot be recorded, so hanging served nobody.

sections.heading: Twenty one languages, finished
sections.body: The app has offered twenty one languages for a while and only English was complete. The next best was German at nineteen per cent, and eight languages sat under nine. Nothing looked broken, because anything missing falls back to English without saying so: a reader in Belgrade or Athens simply found most of the app in a language they had not chosen, after a picker that promised otherwise. Thirty five thousand five hundred and eighty four missing strings are now filled, fifty three thousand across the twenty languages in total, and every one of them was checked before it landed. Finishing the catalogs was not enough on its own, because some of the app never went through them. The prayer rope showed its four prayers in English, so a reader counting knots prayed in English while the same prayer stood translated one screen away. On a phone the Bible index listed Genesis and Matthew in English while the same list on a computer named them correctly, because only the phone had been missed. The sentence above the sign in buttons, the one that makes continuing count as agreeing to the terms, was English for everyone, which is worth more than tidiness: notice a reader cannot read is worth less than none. And the prayer index, the names of the morning rule and Small Compline and the Canon, came out of a table that held English and German and nothing else. Five hundred and fifty nine strings across sixty screens now read from the same catalog as the rest of the app. Counting is not done the same way everywhere and the app now knows it. Arabic has six forms for a number and uses all six, Russian and Polish and Ukrainian need three, and three hundred and forty three of those forms now exist in the catalogs and never will in English. The date above the prayers follows the reader's language too, in that language's own order, so the thirtieth of August is said the way that language says it. All of it is now checked on every build. A missing word, a blank one, a number lost out of the middle of a sentence, an em dash, or a stray piece of HTML markup will stop the build rather than reach a reader.

sections.heading: Four things a reader found
sections.body: A new icon in the shop could not be opened in the app. Tapping it put you on Today, with no error and no explanation, and the odd part was that you could still add it to the cart from the card, which made it look like the product existed and its page did not. That is exactly what was happening. The app carries a page for every icon that existed when the release was built and nothing for one added afterwards, so the shell fell back to its own front door. Icons now open through a fixed address that is always in the app and carries the icon name alongside it, so anything added to the shop opens from now on, including one renamed after a release. The website never had this, because it builds a page on demand and always could. The cart panel had its heading under the phone status bar. It slides in over the whole screen and was measuring from the very top of the glass rather than from below the clock and the battery, so on any phone with a notch the words sat in the strip that is covered. The sign in page had the same fault in a different place: it is the one screen in the app that was never given that measurement at all, so the Purify wordmark and the Privacy link were tucked under the status bar there too. Both now start below it, and on a phone without a notch nothing moves at all. And the saint bump did not work while signed in. Asking for a saint's writings is the one place a reader can tell us what to translate next, and in the app it showed Sign in to request to readers who already were. The app is built before anyone signs in, so the page was deciding at build time that nobody was, and the answer was baked in. It now checks when the page opens instead. Three other things in the same path were fixed with it, because any one of them would have left the button working and the request still failing: the app was calling the site without saying who it was, the server was looking for a signed in reader in the one place the app does not put it, and the browser permission check had nothing to answer it. Worth naming one a reader would have felt: the app also believed nobody had ever bumped anything, so a reader who had already asked for a saint would have seen the button unpressed, pressed it, and quietly withdrawn their own request.

title: The Fathers say what they actually wrote
intro: Purify 1.1 opened Job and Luke. This release is about whether the words already standing under a Father's name are his. In five places they were not, and the largest of them had been there since Job arrived. St Gregory's Morals on the Book of Job, the longest work in the library, was carrying eleven thousand broken characters: every quotation mark in it reached you as a question mark. That is repaired. So is St Cyril's Greek, which had been printing as raw code. And nearly sixteen thousand words that were never patristic text at all have been taken out of the Fathers' mouths, including the title page of one book sitting inside a homily on another, and a Victorian editor's opinion filed under St Gregory. Gregory's Morals can now be read straight through as a book rather than only met a verse at a time, and a chapter with no commentary says so instead of showing you nothing.

sections.heading: Job reads properly
sections.body: St Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job is the largest work in Purify and it arrived damaged. The pages it was taken from are published in an older character set and do not announce it in the way a browser expects, so every curly quotation mark, every apostrophe and every section sign was destroyed on the way in and reached you as a question mark. Seven hundred and ninety five of its nine hundred and twenty notes were affected, eleven thousand one hundred and twenty five characters in all. A reader met sentences like 'by ?the seven sons? is represented the order of the Preachers' throughout the whole of Job. The text has been fetched again and decoded correctly. Nothing was rewritten to repair it: the same nine hundred and twenty notes stand, under the same thirty five books, and the only difference is that the punctuation Gregory's translators printed is now the punctuation you see.

sections.heading: St Cyril speaks Greek again
sections.body: Where the Oxford translators of St Cyril of Alexandria set a phrase in the original Greek, Purify was printing the underlying code instead of the letters, so a line of Cyril on Luke or John could run for half its length as a string of ampersands and numbers. Two thousand six hundred and seventeen of these have been decoded and now read as Greek. The same fault had been quietly deleting other characters without saying so, which had run two words together in Job. Both are fixed.

sections.heading: The back matter is out of the Fathers' mouths
sections.body: These works come to us as scans of printed volumes, and a printed volume does not stop where its author does. It continues into footnote lists, the title page of whatever is bound next, and the editor's own essays. In five places that material had been read as though it were the Father still speaking. Every homily on the First Epistle of John carried its own footnote list as if it were prose, ten thousand eight hundred and fifty seven words of bare Scripture references reading as St Augustine. A note at Matthew 7:21 held four thousand words of the front matter of a different book of Augustine's, its title page and its translator's credits and an introductory essay by its editor. All of it is gone. Nothing of the Fathers went with it: every note that was shortened is word for word what it was, up to the point where the printer stopped and the apparatus began.

sections.heading: A note that was not St Gregory's
sections.body: At Job 38:33 a note ran to seventeen hundred words, and about a thousand of them were not St Gregory. They were a footnote added by the volume's editor in 1844, arguing at length about how Gregory's language on the procession of the Holy Spirit should be read. It carried no mark to say the voice had changed, so it read as Gregory's own words on a question the Church takes seriously. It has been removed. This is a correction of who is speaking and not a judgement about the question itself, which is not something a library settles on its own.

sections.heading: St Gregory's Morals can be read as a book
sections.body: Gregory speaks in more of this commentary than anyone except St John Chrysostom and St Augustine, one thousand one hundred and seventy nine times, and until now his profile held his life and none of his writing. The whole of the Morals on the Book of Job is now on his page, all thirty five books of it, to be read straight through in the order he wrote it rather than only met a verse at a time. It is the longest thing in the library by a wide margin. It opens on his own summary of the first book and ends where he ends, asking that the reader who receives words by his means might give him tears in return.

sections.heading: St Jerome has four of his own works
sections.body: He speaks in eight hundred and fifty one notes of the commentary, third after St John Chrysostom and St Augustine, and his page held his life and nothing he wrote. Four treatises are on it now, from the Oxford translation of 1893: the lives of Paulus the first hermit, of Hilarion who carried the desert into Palestine, and of Malchus, an old man Jerome met in Syria who had been taken by raiders on the road and kept his continence through slavery; and the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary, the treatise in which he answers Helvidius that the brethren of the Lord are His kinsmen and that the Mother of God remained ever virgin. Where the volume's editor introduces a work, that introduction is kept but marked as his, so it is never mistaken for Jerome.

sections.heading: A chapter with nothing says so
sections.body: Some books carry the Fathers on a few chapters and nothing on the rest. Genesis has commentary on one chapter of fifty, Exodus on one of forty, First Samuel on one of thirty one. Until now the other chapters showed nothing at all, with no explanation, so a book marked as having the Fathers looked exactly like a book that has none. One hundred and twenty three chapters now say plainly that there is no commentary for them. The Fathers are not hidden on those pages; there is genuinely nothing there to show, and for most of the Old Testament there never will be, because no translation of it into English exists that is free of copyright.

sections.heading: Where the commentary reaches now
sections.body: Twenty six books of the Bible carry patristic commentary, four hundred and thirty five chapters of the one thousand three hundred and forty six, in twelve thousand and forty five notes. Twenty four voices speak in it and every one of them is venerated by the Church. Every note names its Father, its work and the public-domain edition it was taken from.

title: Luke and Job are opened, and every voice is a saint
intro: Two books that carried no commentary at all are open. Luke now has St Cyril of Alexandria across all twenty four chapters, and Job has St Gregory the Great across all forty two, the largest single work in the library by a wide margin. Cyril's commentary on John arrives as well, the fullest Greek reading of that Gospel that survives. And every name in the commentary is now one the Church venerates: two thousand five hundred and twelve notes standing under nineteen other writers have been taken out. Purify 1.1 also brings in the stylites, the pillar-saints who kept their whole ascetic life on top of a column, gathered under a new heading on the saints index. The Hours page tells you which Hour you are in, days without a saint carry a saying of the Desert Fathers, and search reaches the whole library from your phone.

sections.heading: Luke has the Fathers
sections.body: Luke was the last Gospel with no commentary at all. St John Chrysostom never wrote on it, and the Golden Chain volumes we hold are Matthew and Mark. It now carries St Cyril of Alexandria, one hundred and eighteen sermons reaching every one of the twenty four chapters, with St Augustine beside him. Cyril's Greek survives only in fragments, so what you are reading was preserved whole in Syriac and translated at Oxford in 1859. It is one voice rather than the crowd of Fathers that fills Matthew and Mark, and it is the voice the Church has always read Luke with.

sections.heading: Job is open, and it is the largest thing here
sections.body: Job had nothing. It now carries the whole of St Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job, thirty five books of it, reaching all forty two chapters. It is the longest work in Purify, longer than Chrysostom on Matthew and longer than Augustine on the Psalms. Gregory began it as talks to the brothers who had travelled with him while he was the Pope's representative at Constantinople, and spent years finishing it. It is the book through which the West learned to read Job, and it is far more about the Christian soul under affliction than about the argument of Job's friends. The translation is the Oxford one of 1844.

sections.heading: John has the fullest Greek commentary that survives
sections.body: St Cyril of Alexandria's Commentary on John, twelve books of it, now stands beside St John Chrysostom's homilies and St Augustine's Tractates. Chrysostom preached John to a congregation; Cyril wrote it out. Two of Cyril's twelve books are lost in Greek and are here from the fragments and the Syriac, and the pages say where that is the case. John is now read by nine Fathers.

sections.heading: St Augustine in the pulpit
sections.body: Sermons on Selected Lessons of the Gospels, eighty eight of them, preached to a congregation rather than composed for readers. They read differently from the Tractates for that reason, shorter and more direct. Because Augustine chose his text rather than working through a book, they are spread across Matthew, Mark, Luke and John instead of sitting in one place.

sections.heading: St John Cassian's own words
sections.body: Cassian's profile carried his life and none of his writing. Both of his works are here now, the Institutes and the Conferences, the books through which the prayer of the Egyptian desert reached the West. Three sections are absent and say so on the page: the nineteenth century translators declined to render them, and no other public-domain English of Cassian exists to fill the gap.

sections.heading: Every voice in the commentary is one the Church venerates
sections.body: Most of Matthew and Mark come from the Golden Chain, a thirteenth century Western compilation that quotes whoever served the argument. That included writers the Orthodox Church does not receive as Fathers, works written under borrowed names, and Origen, whose teaching was anathematised at the Fifth Ecumenical Council. Two thousand five hundred and twelve notes standing under nineteen such names have been removed: Origen, Rabanus Maurus, Remigius, the Gloss, Anselm, Ambrosiaster, Haymo of Halberstadt and the rest, together with the Pseudo-Chrysostom, Pseudo-Jerome, Pseudo-Origen and Pseudo-Augustine material. What remains is twenty four voices and every one of them is venerated. Nothing was rewritten and nothing was paraphrased. A note was removed whole or left exactly as it stood.

sections.heading: The scanner's leavings are out of the Fathers' mouths
sections.body: These texts come to us as scans, and a scan carries the whole book: the index of subjects, the index of Scripture references, the concordance to the printed page numbers, the raw list of footnote links. In several places that apparatus had been read as prose and filed under a Father's name at a verse. The worst of them sat at John 21:19, ran to about ninety thousand words, and contained two entire other works that had simply been swept in behind the last tractate. Roughly one hundred and seventy one thousand words of this have been taken out. No commentary was lost with it: John still opens at every verse it opened at before.

sections.heading: The Fathers we quote have pages of their own
sections.body: Eight of the Fathers speaking in the commentary had no profile to tap through to: St Gregory the Great, St Jerome, St Bede, St Hilary of Poitiers, St Ambrose, St Victorinus of Pettau, St Isidore of Seville and St Peter Chrysologus. They have profiles now. None of the eight carries an icon, because no image of them has been opened and checked yet, and an unchecked image is not shipped here.

sections.heading: Where the commentary reaches now
sections.body: Twenty six books of the Bible carry patristic commentary, four hundred and thirty five chapters of the one thousand three hundred and forty six, in twelve thousand and forty eight notes. It was three hundred and sixty nine chapters before this release. Every note names its Father, its work and the public-domain edition it was taken from.

sections.heading: A note on Romans that nobody could open
sections.body: St John Chrysostom's homily on the closing doxology of Romans was filed at Romans 14:25. Our text of that chapter ends at verse 23, so the note sat past the end of the chapter where nothing could reach it. It now sits at Romans 16:25, where the words it quotes actually are.

sections.heading: The pillar-saints have their profiles
sections.body: Symeon the Stylite, Daniel, Symeon of the Wonderful Mountain and Alypius, four men who spent their lives on top of a column in full view of the world. They are gathered under a new Stylites heading on the saints index, and their days in the calendar now open to them. Where the old accounts disagree about a year, the profile says so rather than choosing.

sections.heading: The home page reads straight again
sections.body: On the home page, See today sits level with the Open Purify button again instead of below its middle. The quieter install line under the button had been pulling it down.

sections.heading: Sign in works on iPhone
sections.body: Sign in works on iPhone. The app was throwing your session away on every reload and sending you to the wrong page afterwards, so it looked like signing in had failed.

sections.heading: Light mode is free
sections.body: Light mode is free. It was built months ago, named Parchment, and filed behind Pro by mistake. It is called Light now and everyone has it.

sections.body: Premium Reading Modes moved from Pro to Plus.

sections.heading: The calendar shows today
sections.body: The calendar shows today. On iPhone and Android it was stuck on the day the app was built, and nothing you tapped moved it.

sections.heading: Lenten readings were a week late
sections.body: Lenten readings were a week late. Every Sunday from Zacchaeus to Palm Sunday showed the previous week's Epistle and Gospel. Holy Monday through Holy Saturday now have their own readings.

sections.heading: The calendar is easier on the eyes
sections.body: The calendar is easier on the eyes. It was drawn on pure black with the brightest grey in the palette for its lines. It follows the light and dark themes properly now.

sections.heading: Search works on a phone
sections.body: Search works on a phone. The search index was inside the app the whole time, behind a window that could not open.

sections.heading: Long commentary is readable
sections.body: Long commentary is readable. Two notes were showing a scraper's list of links as if it were St Augustine. Long notes now preview first and tell you the reading time.

sections.heading: A saying on the empty days
sections.body: On the days with no saint profile, a saying of the Desert Fathers appears instead of an empty page.

sections.heading: The Hours tell you which one you are in
sections.body: The Hours page tells you which Hour you are in.

sections.body: The saints of August have their icons.

sections.heading: Saints search was drawn underneath the icons
sections.body: Searching the saints drew the results underneath the icons, so the names were there but unreadable. The same fault affected every dropdown in the app.

sections.heading: Open Purify opens Purify
sections.body: The button that said Open Purify now opens Purify.

sections.body: On the mobile website the last verse of a chapter sat under the reader pill. The spacing meant to prevent that was removing it.

sections.body: The header no longer jumps when you leave the home page.

sections.body: The calendar sends about a fifth of the data it used to, and asks the network three times instead of forty seven.

sections.body: iPhone has its own Plus switch, so a Play Store change cannot affect it.
